notes.definition: A reaction profile (energy level diagram) shows the relative energies of the reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change as a reaction proceeds. Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.
explanation: Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy. The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react is called the activation energy. Collisions between particles with less energy than this do not lead to a reaction; the particles just bounce apart. This is why many reactions, even exothermic ones, need energy to get them started, for example a spark, a flame or heating.

A reaction profile is a diagram that shows how the energy changes as a reaction proceeds. Energy is plotted on the vertical axis and the progress of the reaction on the horizontal axis. The reactants are drawn as a horizontal line on the left and the products as a horizontal line on the right. A curved line joins them, rising to a peak. The difference between the reactant level and the peak is the activation energy. The difference between the reactant and product levels is the overall energy change.

In an exothermic reaction, the products are at a lower energy than the reactants. The difference in energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the overall energy change arrow points downwards from the reactants to the products. In an endothermic reaction, the products are at a higher energy than the reactants because energy has been taken in from the surroundings. The overall energy change arrow points upwards from the reactants to the products.

You can use a reaction profile to identify whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic: just compare the heights of the reactant and product lines. Products lower means exothermic; products higher means endothermic. The size of the activation energy does not tell you which type the reaction is. A reaction with a large activation energy can still be strongly exothermic, such as the combustion of methane, which needs a flame or spark to start.

When drawing a reaction profile, label both axes (energy and progress of reaction), label the reactants and products, draw a smooth curve that rises above both levels, and draw arrows for the activation energy (from the reactant line up to the peak) and the overall energy change (from the reactant line to the product line). If values are given, you can read off the activation energy and overall energy change by subtraction.
keyFacts: Reactions only happen when particles collide with sufficient energy.
Activation energy is the minimum energy particles must have to react.
A reaction profile plots energy (y-axis) against progress of reaction (x-axis).
Exothermic profile: products lower in energy than reactants.
Endothermic profile: products higher in energy than reactants.
Activation energy is measured from the reactant level up to the peak of the curve.
Overall energy change is the difference between the reactant and product levels.
The arrow for overall energy change points down for exothermic and up for endothermic reactions.
Exothermic reactions can still need energy to start, because of activation energy.

keyTerms.definition: The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.
A diagram showing the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change as the reaction proceeds.
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products.
Particles hitting each other; only collisions with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy lead to a reaction.
The label on the horizontal axis of a reaction profile, showing the reaction moving from reactants to products.

equations.name: Activation energy from a profile
equations.formula: activation energy = energy at the peak − energy of reactants

equations.name: Overall energy change from a profile
equations.formula: overall energy change = energy of products − energy of reactants (negative for exothermic)

workedExamples.title: Reading an exothermic profile
workedExamples.question: On a reaction profile the reactants are at 100 kJ, the peak of the curve is at 180 kJ and the products are at 40 kJ. Find the activation energy and the overall energy change.
steps: Overall energy change = products − reactants = 40 − 100 = −60 kJ.
The products are lower than the reactants, so energy is released.
workedExamples.answer: Activation energy 80 kJ; 60 kJ released (−60 kJ), so the reaction is exothermic.

workedExamples.title: Reading an endothermic profile
workedExamples.question: The reactants are at 30 kJ, the peak is at 150 kJ and the products are at 75 kJ. Find the activation energy and the overall energy change.
steps: The products are higher than the reactants, so energy is taken in.
workedExamples.answer: Activation energy 120 kJ; 45 kJ taken in (+45 kJ), so the reaction is endothermic.

workedExamples.title: Drawing a profile from a description
workedExamples.question: Describe how to draw the reaction profile for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, which is endothermic.
steps: Draw and label the axes: energy (vertical) and progress of reaction (horizontal).
Draw a short horizontal line on the left labelled CaCO₃ (reactants).
Draw a higher horizontal line on the right labelled CaO + CO₂ (products).
Join them with a curve that rises above both lines.
Add an upward arrow from the reactant line to the peak labelled activation energy, and an upward arrow from the reactant line to the product line labelled energy taken in.
workedExamples.answer: A profile with the products higher than the reactants, a hump above both, and labelled arrows for activation energy and overall energy change.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often measure activation energy from the products to the peak.
misconceptions.right: In fact activation energy is measured from the reactant level to the peak of the curve.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a reaction that needs heating to start must be endothermic.
misconceptions.right: In fact all reactions have an activation energy. Whether a reaction is exothermic depends only on whether the products are lower in energy than the reactants.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the overall energy change is the height of the peak.
misconceptions.right: In fact the overall energy change is the difference between the reactant and product levels.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think any collision between particles leads to a reaction.
misconceptions.right: In fact particles only react if they collide with energy at least equal to the activation energy.

realWorld: Natural gas does not burn in air until a spark or flame supplies the activation energy, which is why gas cookers have igniters.
Safety matches need friction to supply the activation energy for the reactions in the match head.
Fuel and air in a car engine are ignited by a spark plug; once started, the exothermic combustion keeps going.
examTips: Always label both axes, the reactants, the products, the activation energy and the overall energy change on a reaction profile.
Draw the activation energy arrow starting at the reactant line, not at the x-axis.
Make sure the curve rises above both the reactant and product lines.
To decide exothermic or endothermic, compare reactants and products only; ignore the height of the peak.
Use subtraction to read values off a profile and give the unit (usually kJ or kJ/mol).
summary: Particles react only if they collide with energy at least equal to the activation energy.
A reaction profile plots energy against progress of reaction.
Exothermic: products lower than reactants; energy released.
Endothermic: products higher than reactants; energy taken in.
Activation energy: reactants up to the peak.
Overall energy change: difference between reactants and products.

questions.question: What is meant by activation energy?
options: The minimum energy particles must have to react
The energy released when a reaction finishes
The energy stored in the products
The total energy of the reactants
markScheme: 1 mark: the minimum energy particles must have to react
questions.explanation: Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for colliding particles to react. It is not the energy released or the energy of the products.

questions.question: On the reaction profile for an exothermic reaction, where are the products?
options: Higher in energy than the reactants
At the same energy as the reactants
Lower in energy than the reactants
At the top of the curve
markScheme: 1 mark: lower in energy than the reactants
questions.explanation: In an exothermic reaction energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the products end up with less energy than the reactants.

questions.question: What label should go on the horizontal axis of a reaction profile?
options: Temperature
Time in seconds
Energy
Progress of reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: progress of reaction
questions.explanation: Energy goes on the vertical axis. The horizontal axis shows the reaction proceeding from reactants to products, so it is labelled progress of reaction.

questions.question: On the reaction profile for an endothermic reaction, which way does the arrow for the overall energy change point?
options: Downwards from reactants to products
Upwards from reactants to products
Upwards from products to the peak
Downwards from the peak to the products
markScheme: 1 mark: upwards from reactants to products
questions.explanation: In an endothermic reaction the products have more energy than the reactants, so the arrow goes up from the reactant level to the product level.

questions.question: The combustion of methane is exothermic, but a gas cooker needs a spark to light the gas. Why?
options: Combustion of methane is really endothermic
The spark makes the products lower in energy
The spark provides the energy released by the reaction
The spark gives particles enough energy to overcome the activation energy
markScheme: 1 mark: the spark supplies the activation energy
questions.explanation: Even exothermic reactions have an activation energy. The spark gives some particles enough energy to react; the energy released then keeps the reaction going.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows information about two reactions, A and B.
Which statement is correct?
options: Reaction A is more likely to start at room temperature because its activation energy is lower
Reaction B is more likely to start at room temperature because it releases more energy
Reaction A is endothermic because it releases less energy
Both reactions need the same energy to start because both are exothermic
markScheme: 1 mark: A is more likely to start because its activation energy is lower
questions.explanation: Whether a reaction starts easily depends on the activation energy, not on how much energy is released. Both reactions are exothermic because both overall energy changes are negative.

questions.question: A student says: 'This reaction has a very large activation energy, so it must be endothermic.' Which statement is correct?
options: The student is right, because energy must be taken in to start the reaction
The student is right, because the peak is higher than the products
The student is wrong, because exothermic or endothermic depends on the relative energies of reactants and products
The student is wrong, because endothermic reactions have no activation energy
markScheme: 1 mark: the student is wrong; it depends on the relative energies of reactants and products
questions.explanation: All reactions have an activation energy, whether exothermic or endothermic. Only the comparison of reactant and product energy decides the type.

questions.question: When a reaction takes place in a test tube, the tube feels colder. What would the reaction profile show?
options: Products lower in energy than reactants
No activation energy
Reactants and products at the same energy
Products higher in energy than reactants
markScheme: 1 mark: products higher in energy than reactants
questions.explanation: The tube feels colder because the reaction takes in energy from the surroundings. This is endothermic, so the products are higher in energy than the reactants.

An exothermic reaction has these energy values:
• the reactants are at 120 kJ
• the products have 85 kJ less energy than the reactants
• the activation energy is 35 kJ.
Calculate the energy at the peak of the reaction profile.
markScheme: 1 mark: peak = reactants + activation energy
questions.explanation: The peak is the activation energy above the reactant level: 120 + 35 = 155 kJ. The 85 kJ released is not needed for this calculation.

questions.question: Define activation energy.
markScheme: 1 mark: the minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react
questions.explanation: The key word is minimum. Particles with less energy than this bounce apart without reacting.

questions.question: Give two things that a reaction profile shows.
acceptedAnswers: relative energies of reactants and products
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: relative energies of reactants and products; activation energy; overall energy change (energy released or taken in)
questions.explanation: A reaction profile shows the energy of the reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change.

questions.question: On a reaction profile, the products are drawn higher than the reactants. State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
markScheme: 1 mark: endothermic
questions.explanation: Products higher than reactants means energy has been taken in from the surroundings, so the reaction is endothermic.

questions.question: Explain how a reaction profile shows that a reaction is exothermic.
markScheme: 1 mark: the products are at a lower energy than the reactants
1 mark: so the difference in energy has been transferred (released) to the surroundings
questions.explanation: The products have less energy than the reactants. The missing energy was transferred to the surroundings.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of particles, why reactions can only happen when particles collide with sufficient energy.
acceptedAnswers: energy at least the activation energy
markScheme: 1 mark: particles must collide to react
1 mark: the collision must have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy; collisions with less energy do not lead to a reaction
questions.explanation: Only collisions with at least the activation energy result in a reaction. Other collisions do not have enough energy, so the particles simply bounce apart.

questions.question: Calcium carbonate decomposes when heated: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The reaction is endothermic. Describe the reaction profile for this reaction.
acceptedAnswers: activation energy from reactants to peak
axes energy and progress of reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: reactants (CaCO₃) lower and products (CaO + CO₂) higher
1 mark: a curve that rises to a peak above both levels, with activation energy shown from reactants to peak
1 mark: overall energy change shown as an upward arrow from reactants to products (energy taken in)
questions.explanation: For an endothermic reaction the product line is higher than the reactant line. The activation energy and overall energy change arrows both start from the reactant level.

questions.question: Once the combustion of a fuel has started, it continues without any more heating. Explain why.
acceptedAnswers: provides activation energy for further particles
markScheme: 1 mark: the reaction is exothermic and releases energy
1 mark: this energy gives more reactant particles enough energy to overcome the activation energy, so the reaction keeps going
questions.explanation: The spark only supplies the activation energy at the start. The energy released by the reaction then supplies the activation energy for more particles.

questions.question:
A company wants to use a reaction in a hand warmer.
Table 1 shows information about three reactions, P, Q and R.
Suggest which reaction would be best for a hand warmer.
Explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: P
1 mark: it is exothermic (releases energy) and has a low activation energy so it starts easily at room temperature; Q needs too much energy to start and R is endothermic
questions.explanation: A hand warmer must release energy, which rules out R. Q releases a similar amount of energy to P but has a very high activation energy, so it would not start without heating.

questions.question: Compare the reaction profiles of an exothermic reaction and an endothermic reaction. In your answer describe the features of each profile and explain what they show about the energy changes.
markScheme: Indicative content: both profiles have energy on the y-axis and progress of reaction on the x-axis; both show reactants on the left and products on the right; both have a curve that rises to a peak; activation energy is shown in both from the reactant level to the peak; activation energy is the minimum energy particles need to react; exothermic: products lower than reactants; overall energy change arrow points down; energy transferred to the surroundings, so temperature of surroundings increases; endothermic: products higher than reactants; arrow points up; energy taken in from the surroundings, so temperature of surroundings decreases; the height of the peak does not decide whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear comparison of both profiles with similarities and differences, correct use of activation energy and overall energy change, and links to energy transfer to or from the surroundings.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes both profiles with some correct features, with some explanation of energy changes.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or both profiles, for example products lower for exothermic.
questions.explanation: The key difference is the position of the products relative to the reactants. Both profiles share the same axes and both show an activation energy, which explains why both types of reaction may need energy to start.

questions.question: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gases can be kept at room temperature without reacting. When a spark is applied, the mixture explodes and forms water in a strongly exothermic reaction. Explain these observations using ideas about collisions and activation energy. You may refer to a reaction profile.
markScheme: Indicative content: at room temperature the particles collide but very few collisions have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy; so there is no (noticeable) reaction; the activation energy is high; the spark gives some particles enough energy to overcome the activation energy, so they react; the reaction is exothermic and releases a large amount of energy; this energy gives more particles enough energy to react, so the reaction spreads very quickly (explosion); on a reaction profile, the products (water) are much lower than the reactants and the peak is well above the reactants.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation linking activation energy to both the lack of reaction at room temperature and the effect of the spark, with the role of the energy released.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example the spark provides energy, with limited explanation.
questions.explanation: The mixture is stable at room temperature because collisions do not have enough energy to reach the activation energy. The spark starts the reaction, and the large amount of energy released supplies the activation energy for the rest of the mixture.
